opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's strange mainly because the setup is so different from the domains most of us grew up on, like language or vision. In language modeling, you have a sequence of tokens, and the task is pretty well defined: predict the next token. The input and output live in the same space, and there's a natural structure you can exploit. Retrieval and recommendation don't really work that way.

In recommender systems, a lot of your "vocabulary" is just item IDs. These are arbitrary identifiers that carry no inherent meaning. Item 4,512 has no semantic relationship to item 4,513, unlike words, which have morphology, context, and shared meaning. So you end up with these massive embedding tables where most of the model's capacity sits in memorizing IDs rather than learning generalizable structure. That always felt a bit unnatural to me. It's less "modeling" in the classical sense and more giant lookup tables with some interaction layers on top.

Retrieval has a similar oddness. Traditionally it's framed as: encode the query, encode the documents, then do nearest-neighbor search in some vector space. The model and the index are two separate things, and the index sits outside the neural network. That made us ask, why can't the model just be the index? Why can't you train one model that, given a query, directly generates the identifier of the relevant document? That was the motivation behind the Differentiable Search Index work, treating retrieval as a sequence-to-sequence problem where the corpus is encoded in the model's parameters.

Once you go down that path, the strangeness gets more interesting. You have to decide how to represent document IDs. Do you use arbitrary atomic IDs, or do you build semantically structured IDs, for example by clustering documents hierarchically so similar documents share prefixes? That choice matters a lot, because you're essentially designing a vocabulary that the model must learn to "speak." In language, the vocabulary is given. Here you invent it, and invention is hard.

There's also the evaluation and data side. In recommendation, the signals are implicit and noisy: clicks, watch time, skips. Feedback loops abound, since the system shapes the data it later trains on. So it's not a clean supervised learning problem; it's almost a mix of supervised learning, bandits, and systems engineering.

So, to me, the strangeness boils down to this: these domains have historically been treated as matching or lookup problems, not generative modeling problems. Part of the fun has been asking whether the generative, unified-model paradigm that worked so well in language can be brought over, and what breaks when you try.

r001.rationale: The response describes arbitrary item IDs, an external retrieval index, noisy feedback, and feedback loops, but it does not attribute the strangeness to a perceived distance between modeling actions and their effects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the strange thing about recommenders and IR is that there's no real ground truth in the way you have it in, say, vision or even language. If you're doing image classification, a cat is a cat. The label is kind of a property of the world. But in recommendation, the labels are basically a byproduct of some system that was already running. A user clicked on something because the previous model showed it to them, in that position, at that time, on that screen. So you're learning from data that your own system generated, and the thing you're trying to predict is partly a function of what you did before. It's this weird feedback loop where the dataset isn't really a dataset, it's more like a log of your own past decisions.

And then the other thing is that the IDs don't mean anything. In language, a token carries some semantic content that transfers. In a recommender, item 47382 is just an index. There's no reason that structure should generalize to another platform, or even to the same platform six months later, because the catalog churns and user behavior drifts. So you spend a huge amount of effort on things like embedding tables, hashing, cold start, and none of that is really about understanding anything. It's about managing this constantly moving target.

So coming from that world and then moving into language modeling, it honestly felt almost relaxing. You train on text, the text stays text, and the thing you're modeling has some stable structure underneath it. Whereas in recsys I always had this feeling that I was modeling an artifact of the product rather than any real phenomenon. That's what made it feel strange to me, that so much of the field was very sophisticated machinery pointed at a target that kept moving because the machinery itself was moving it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the strangeness to feedback loops and labels shaped by prior system decisions, but does not clearly identify a perceived distance between modeling actions and their effects.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s strange is that, in recommendation, the things you’re modeling are often just IDs. You have a user ID and an item ID, and you’re trying to learn something meaningful from their interactions. There isn’t necessarily an intrinsic structure to those IDs. If you rename them consistently, the problem stays the same. That feels very different from language or images, where the input itself has a lot of structure.

And in information retrieval, even when you have text, relevance is relational. A document isn’t relevant in isolation; it’s relevant to a particular query, for a particular person, in a particular context. The supervision is also often indirect. A click might mean something was useful, or it might just mean it was shown first. So you’re modeling this mixture of content, human behavior, and the system that decided what people got to see. That makes it a very interesting modeling problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes ID-based inputs, relational relevance, and noisy clicks shaped by exposure, but it does not clearly attribute the strangeness to a distance between modeling actions and their effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s strange is that, in recommendation, the things you’re modeling are often just IDs. You have a user ID and an item ID, and you learn embeddings for them from interactions. Unlike words or pixels, those IDs don’t have any intrinsic meaning. If you permute them consistently, the problem is exactly the same. But somehow you’re learning this very rich structure about people’s preferences from that.

Information retrieval has a similar tension. You have language on both sides—a query and a document—but the objective isn’t simply to understand the language. It’s to decide which document is relevant to this particular query, often using fairly sparse signals about what relevance means. And the collection itself can keep changing.

So I find these domains interesting because you’re not just modeling an object. You’re modeling relationships: between users and items, or queries and documents. A lot of the meaning comes from those relationships, rather than from the individual inputs.

r001.rationale: The response says recommendation IDs lack intrinsic meaning and that structure is learned from interactions, but it does not attribute the domains’ strangeness to a distance between modeling actions and their effects.
